prompt.context: A major East Coast, vertically integrated and regulated electric utility has received a permit to build its first nuclear power plant.
prompt.question: The client wants to know if building this nuclear power plant will be a good investment and what risks are associated with this venture.

clarifying_info.q: Can you describe the structure of the company? What does 'vertically integrated' and 'regulated' mean?
clarifying_info.a: A vertically integrated utility owns the entire value chain – generation, transmission and distribution. It is somewhat of a monopoly and is overseen by state regulators.
There is virtually no competition because it is a regulated industry.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the plant?
clarifying_info.a: The new plant is expected to supply about 8,760 GWh (Gigawatt hours) per year and it is expected to be utilized for 30 years.
The current annual demand in the utility's service area is 17,000 GWh. For this case assume this demand will remain constant in the near future.

clarifying_info.q: What is the expected revenue on a variable basis?
What is the expected variable cost?
Why is the utility building this new plant?
clarifying_info.a: Currently the company has about 9,000 GWh of supply that comes from old, dirty and inefficient coal fired power plants. It plans to retire them in the near future.
The utility plans to outsource the building of the nuclear plant and the price quote is about $7 Billion.

clarifying_info.q: What is the market cap of the client?
clarifying_info.a: The market cap of this company is $6 Billion.

framework: Understand company structure and industry: regulated monopoly, entire value chain owned, state oversight
Assess the need for the project: retiring ~9,000 GWh of old coal capacity, current demand 17,000 GWh
Calculate expected total fixed cost including cost overrun risk (expected value of capital outlay)
Evaluate revenue streams and contribution margin to determine annual cash generation
Calculate breakeven period and compare to industry benchmarks
Identify financial risks: project cost vs. market cap, debt/equity financing burden, capital constraints
Identify organizational risks: skilled nuclear workforce availability, training costs, safety and reliability

questions.prompt: Phase 1: What is the expected value of the total cost of the plant given construction cost overrun risks?
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply expected value logic: base cost plus probability-weighted overrun for each construction component.

math.setup: Base cost $7B. Three components with independent overrun probabilities: Technology & engineering ($4B base, 50% risk, $800M overrun), Structure ($2B base, 50% risk, $600M overrun), Other overhead ($1B base, 20% risk, $250M overrun).

questions.prompt: Phase 2: What is the annual contribution margin from the plant, and what is the breakeven period?
questions.guidance: Candidate should convert units (GWh to MWh), calculate contribution per MWh, multiply by annual capacity, then divide expected fixed cost by annual contribution.

math.setup: Capacity: 8,760 GWh/year = 8,760,000 MWh/year. Revenue: $80/MWh. Variable cost: $10/MWh.

questions.prompt: Phase 3: What are the key financial and organizational risks?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note: (1) plant cost ($7.75B) exceeds market cap ($6B) — must raise more than company is worth; (2) breakeven of ~13 years vs industry average 6–7 years; (3) heavy reliance on debt or expensive equity; (4) other capital investment crowded out; (5) shortage of skilled nuclear personnel; (6) significant training and hiring costs; (7) safety and reliability concerns with complex nuclear technology.

recommendation: The client should NOT proceed with this nuclear power plant investment at this time.

The expected total construction cost is $7.75B — more than the company's entire market cap of $6B — and the breakeven period is approximately 13 years, nearly double the industry average of 6–7 years.
risks: Financial risk: the project requires raising capital in excess of the firm's current market value, necessitating heavy debt or dilutive equity financing that will constrain future investments
Cost overrun risk: expected overruns add $750M above the $7B quote
Organizational risk: shortage of personnel with nuclear expertise requires significant time and cost to hire and train
Safety and reliability risk inherent to nuclear technology operation
next_steps: Evaluate alternative, less expensive generation technologies (e.g., natural gas, renewables) to replace the retiring coal fleet
Assess whether a smaller phased investment or partnership/co-ownership structure could reduce financial exposure
Conduct a workforce capability assessment to understand the gap in nuclear-qualified personnel
